5.3 Temporal Backtesting, Baselines, and Conditions of Failure
The proposal is scientific only if temporal backtests, contrastive datasets, ablations, human
studies, and simpler baselines can prove it wrong.
The first empirical challenge is to construct a corpus and annotation regime without turning the initial ontology into the conclusion. A dataset of “ideas” cannot be sampled in the same way as images of already named objects. Curators must decide where one contribution ends and another begins, which relations matter, and which sources count as evidence. These decisions should be treated as experimental material rather than hidden preprocessing.
A suitable corpus should begin with bounded scientific episodes. A good episode contains a tractable lineage, diverse source types, meaningful technical variation, and experts capable of reconstructing the history. Examples might include a family of optimisation methods, an experimental technique that migrated across disciplines, a causal-inference design, or a scientific concept whose terminology changed. The first objective is not representativeness of all science. It is enough variation to stress the theory of identity while preserving the possibility of close verification.
The corpus must include more than canonical papers. Reviews and textbooks reveal how fields retrospectively organise a lineage. Code and protocols reveal operational details absent from articles. Older books, proceedings, theses, patents, and archives may contain earlier attestations. Negative results and failed applications expose conditions of validity. Multilingual material is essential whenever priority or conceptual migration crosses linguistic traditions. Source selection should be documented as part of the dataset, including known gaps.
Annotation should proceed from evidence to interpretations. Curators first identify addressable attestations: passages, equations, diagrams, code fragments, or artefacts. They then propose role structures and relation claims. This order prevents the abstraction from losing its documentary anchor. Each annotation records the task and granularity at which it was produced. An expert may annotate the same passage differently for a mechanism comparison and for a historical study; both can be valid.
The protocol should collect alternative decompositions rather than force agreement too early. Inter-annotator disagreement can reveal ambiguous boundaries, ontology defects, or genuine pluralism. Conventional agreement statistics remain useful, but low agreement should not automatically be treated as annotator failure. The dataset needs a disagreement taxonomy distinguishing accidental inconsistency from different legitimate models. Adjudication should record the reasons for preferring one view in a particular benchmark.
Contrastive examples are more valuable than large quantities of easy positives. The corpus should include pairs with similar wording but different mechanisms, different wording but equivalent functions, shared mechanisms with independent histories, and apparent novelty caused by missing sources. It should also include transformations that alter only one role. These cases test whether a system has learned typed identity rather than generic semantic proximity.
Multi-resolution annotation is essential. Curators can provide a coarse operational object, a finer decomposition, and relations between them. The dataset then supports experiments on whether a model chooses an appropriate level for the question. It also enables evaluation of stability: does a claimed lineage survive refinement, or was it an artefact of coarse representation?
Historical claims require a different evidence protocol from semantic ones. An influence annotation should cite documentary or contextual support, not merely a similarity judgment. A priority annotation should describe the corpus searched and the dating basis. Independent rediscovery should remain provisional when transmission evidence is incomplete. These requirements make annotation slower, but they are necessary if the atlas is to support more than semantic search.
Existing resources provide valuable starting points. IdeaGene-Bench supplies typed objects and lineage differences across ten domains (Zhou et al. 2026). RINoBench provides expert judgments of research idea novelty (Schopf and Färber 2026). CHIMERA supplies mined recombination cases (Sternlicht and Hope 2026). Scideator and literature-grounded novelty work provide facet structures and retrieval protocols (Radensky et al. 2024; Shahid et al. 2025). The atlas research programme should reuse these resources while adding source-addressed evidence, alternative decompositions, typed uncertainty, and temporal corpus boundaries.
The resulting dataset should be regarded as a set of arguments, not only labels. A benchmark instance includes the source material, the operational representations, the relation under test, the supporting and opposing evidence, and the adjudication context. This richer form makes evaluation more demanding but reduces the risk that systems optimise against unexplained judgments.
A broad end-to-end demonstration cannot reveal which part of the atlas is scientifically responsible for an improvement. The research programme needs a family of benchmarks aligned with the conceptual distinctions developed in earlier chapters. Each benchmark should compare against strong document-level, embedding, graph, and language-model baselines.
Idea decomposition tests whether a system can propose useful role structures from sources. Evaluation should measure span grounding, role correctness, structural relations, and the ability to represent alternatives. Exact graph match is informative but too strict when several decompositions are legitimate. Pairwise expert comparison and task performance can supplement it.

Chapter 6. Critics, Review, Compliance, and Scientific Sovereignty
Correction becomes real only when it is embodied in institutions and software that can oppose a claim. This chapter groups the technologies that produce, preserve, and adjudicate criticism:
independent critics, dependency fingerprints, severe-test designers, causal challenge,
replication, validity dossiers, peer review, evidential escalation, compliance, privacy, copyright, controlled data use, release gates, and appeal. These functions cannot be collapsed into one
score or one model. Their scientific value depends on independence, typed evidence,
transparent authority, and the possibility that a decision can be contested by actors who do not
share the same incentives or infrastructure.

spans.quote:
6.4 Power, Infrastructure, Appeal, and Scientific Sovereignty
Control of models, corpora, compute, laboratories, standards, and data can determine which
questions are visible and who can challenge the answers.
In stories about automated science, the spectacular moment is discovery: the agent proposes a molecule, finds a law, or uncovers a hidden connection. Less visible is the earlier moment when someone decides which problem deserves to be solved. That choice precedes the data. It distributes attention, money, time, and risk. Calling a system autonomous without asking who defined its objective confuses freedom of execution with freedom of purpose.
Axiology is the study of value, and science contains values even when it claims neutrality. Epistemic values such as accuracy, simplicity, explanatory power, scope, and robustness guide theory choice. Social and moral values enter the selection of topics, the design of risk thresholds, and the interpretation of consequences. Heather Douglas has argued that when uncertainty affects decisions with social consequences, scientists cannot avoid value judgement entirely; they can only make it more or less visible and accountable (Douglas, 2009).
An AI receives values as objectives, constraints, examples, and reward signals. Asked to maximize yield, it treats measured yield as good. Asked to minimize cost, it notices the costs represented in the model and ignores those outside it. A drug-discovery agent evaluated by commercially promising candidates may favour diseases with clear biomarkers, strong datasets, and viable markets. Rare diseases, preventive interventions, non-patentable therapies, or conditions concentrated among poor populations may receive less attention not because they matter less, but because the infrastructure makes them harder to optimize.
This is politics embedded in engineering. It requires no conspiracy. Companies use metrics compatible with their business models. Public agencies follow mandates. Laboratories ask questions their instruments can answer. AI amplifies these preferences by exploring the chosen direction at high velocity. A slight initial tilt becomes a motorway.
The agenda of science has never been a neutral list of puzzles. Maternal health, neglected tropical disease, subsistence agriculture, low-resource languages, disability, environmental exposure, and the long-term maintenance of public infrastructure can remain underfunded despite enormous social importance. Their data may be fragmented and their benefits diffuse. An agent trained to predict publication, citation, patentability, or return on investment will reproduce this distribution efficiently without possessing any psychological prejudice.
The same technology can alter the economy. Lower costs of synthesis, modelling, and software may let small teams investigate questions previously reserved for wealthy institutions. Public-interest agents can compare disease burden with research investment, identify communities absent from datasets, or search systematically for promising ideas that lack commercial sponsors. Funders can reserve part of a portfolio for uncertainty, equity, replication, and public goods rather than maximizing near-term probability of success.
Democratization is therefore a design choice, not an automatic consequence of cheaper intelligence. It depends on access to models, compute, literature, laboratories, training, and channels of publication. It also depends on who can set objectives. Giving a community a chatbot while retaining control over data, tools, and research priorities elsewhere is not epistemic self-determination.
Citizen science offers another possible architecture. Millions of people already observe birds, classify galaxies, monitor water, report symptoms, transcribe archives, and contribute spare attention to problems no professional team could cover alone. AI can translate protocols, adapt interfaces to different abilities and languages, triage observations, detect anomalies, and return local explanations to participants. It can make collective intelligence more continuous: a community notices a pattern, an agent compares it with the literature, a laboratory designs a test, and the result returns to the place where the question began (Bonney et al., 2014).
This opportunity has an exploitative version. A platform can call people citizen scientists while treating them as unpaid sensors, extracting data and intellectual value without shared governance, attribution, or benefit. Automated quality control can also erase observations that do not fit the model, precisely where local knowledge might reveal that the model is incomplete. Genuine participation requires the right to shape questions, inspect how contributions are used, contest classifications, withdraw sensitive data, and share in the resulting infrastructure or value. AI should not merely harvest a wider public; it can help make the public a more powerful author and critic of research.
Question selection should be separated from method selection. Agents can help map needs, knowledge gaps, tractability, possible harms, and neglected opportunities. They can calculate scenarios and expose trade-offs. Publicly consequential priorities require deliberation among people with legitimate standing. A model can estimate potential lives saved. It cannot decide by technical competence alone how much inequality is acceptable, which risks may be imposed, or what obligations are owed to future generations.
Dual use makes the issue acute. Knowledge in biology, chemistry, cyber systems, materials, and behavioural science can support benefit and harm. An agent capable of planning a valuable experiment may also lower the expertise required for dangerous work. Safety cannot consist only of blocking certain words. A capable system can decompose a goal, use indirect language, or combine benign tools into a harmful path. Identity, authorization, contextual evaluation, monitoring, and tool-leve

Chapter 9. Human-Governed Artificial Science
Keeping people at the helm cannot mean asking for a ceremonial click after machines have
selected the question, spent the resources, produced the evidence, and defined the options.
Human command must be expressed through purpose, rights, limits, appeal, responsibility, and
benefit. This chapter examines the emerging AI scientist, the ladder from assistance to
autonomy, the possibility of artificial scientific communities, the risk of automated monoculture,
and the institutions needed to keep heterogeneous human and machine capacities inside a
republic of knowledge rather than a platform empire.
spans.sectionHeading: Chapter 9. Human-Governed Artificial Science

spans.quote:
9.5 Human Command, Responsibility, Credit, and Benefit
Human command should not be confused with the requirement that a person click approve at the end of an automated process. Command exists only when people or legitimate institutions retain meaningful authority over purpose, constraints, irreversible actions, release, and the distribution of consequences. They must receive evidence that is adequate for the decision, possess enough time and competence to interpret it, be able to stop or redirect the process, and have a path for appeal. A nominal human in the loop who cannot reconstruct how a claim was produced or alter the system's course is a liability holder, not a commander.
A Constitution of Decision Rights
Scientific automation requires a constitution because different actions carry different kinds of authority. An agent may be allowed to search literature, generate code in a sandbox, or propose experiments without permission for every step. It should not automatically be allowed to purchase materials, expose research subjects, change a clinical protocol, publish a high-consequence claim, or deploy a technology. Decision rights can be attached to action classes, resource thresholds, risk profiles, evidence states, and named institutional roles. The constitutional layer should be inspectable and versioned, so that a change in authority is itself an event in the research record.
This architecture should support delegation without pretending that every decision can be anticipated. When a process encounters a novel action or a conflict among rules, it must abstain and escalate. Escalation should include the relevant claim-evidence path, uncertainties, alternatives, expected consequences, and the reason the existing policy is insufficient. The research problem is to determine whether such evidence packages genuinely improve human judgment or merely overwhelm reviewers with machine-produced detail. Interfaces should therefore be evaluated through decision quality, reconstruction time, missed harms, and the ability of decision-makers to identify when the system framed the problem incorrectly.
The Researcher as Architect of Correctability
As implementation, search, and routine analysis become cheaper, the researcher's contribution shifts toward the architecture of inquiry. This includes deciding which uncertainty matters, choosing or inventing representations, identifying sources of independent resistance, designing evaluators that cannot be satisfied by superficial optimization, and determining which consequences require public or specialist authorization. These are not uniquely human capacities in principle. They are the capacities that remain scarce when local generation and execution are abundant, regardless of whether they are eventually exercised by people, machines, or mixed institutions.
Coding agents make this shift visible. A small team can create a prototype that would once have required a large implementation effort. The resulting temptation is to treat fluent implementation as evidence that the underlying research question has been clarified. In fact, faster implementation increases the cost of conceptual negligence. The researcher must specify invariants, test boundaries, provenance, threat models, data rights, fallback behavior, and conditions of abandonment before the first successful demonstration becomes the de facto architecture. Books, design arguments, executable specifications, adversarial examples, and early prototypes become complementary instruments of preparation.
The role should also retain direct contact with failure. Excessive delegation can deskill researchers until they can no longer distinguish a surprising result from a broken pipeline or a plausible mechanism from an artefact of the evaluator. Critical nodes therefore need deliberate human practice: inspecting raw measurements, reproducing selected analyses independently, challenging model assumptions, and conducting periodic manual or alternative-tool audits. The objective is not nostalgia for manual work. It is to preserve enough competence for oversight to remain substantive.
Credit, Responsibility, and Benefit
A single authorship label will increasingly misrepresent distributed research. Contributions may include problem framing, data creation, instrument operation, model design, code generation, experimental execution, criticism, replication, compliance review, community participation, and decisions that prevented an unsafe release. A research object should record these contributions without implying that all are equivalent. It should also preserve responsibility: who authorized an action, who controlled the model or data, who could have stopped the process, and who had access to the evidence required for the decision.
Human command must also include the distribution of benefit. Automated science can concentrate returns in the owners of models, compute, data, laboratories, and validation infrastructure while externalizing risk to subjects, workers, public institutions, and communities that supplied the data. A research object should therefore preserve not only technical contribution but claims about authorship, data rights, community participation, licensing, public value, and responsibility. Benefit-sharing will remain a political choice, but infrastructure can make the choice explicit and contestable rather than allowing the default ownership stack to decide it invisibly.
This requirement is not a demand that software determine justice. It is a demand that the system stop erasing the information needed for a political and ethical decision. Data-use conditions, community agreements, public funding, intellectual-property assignments, environmental cost, and downstream revenue can be linked to the same project history that records scientific contributions. Different institutions may choose different benefit rules, but the decision should not be made accidentally by whichever contract or platform happen

10.1 Research Objects, Specifications, Memory, Novelty, and Relevance
The first family of projects concerns the scientific object itself. Contemporary research is still organised around papers, repositories, notebooks, and databases that expose fragments of an inquiry but not the semantic trajectory by which claims changed. The research question is whether a durable, evidence-bearing object can make scientific correction computationally tractable without pretending that every concept is already formal. The work is not primarily a new file format. It is the construction of a layer in which claims, evidence, reasons, negative results, uncertainty, and decisions can be linked, versioned, queried, and selectively recomputed.

The central hypothesis is that a scientific project can be represented at a level between raw event logging and retrospective narrative. The object must preserve claims, assumptions, evidence, objections, negative branches, environments, and decisions without requiring every domain to accept one exhaustive ontology. A small common kernel may describe identity, provenance, scope, support, opposition, dependency, uncertainty, and authority. Domain extensions can then represent a proof obligation, a laboratory calibration, a clinical endpoint, a qualitative coding decision, or a model-selection event. The research challenge is to discover whether this layered representation remains coherent when the same claim moves among disciplines and forms of evidence.
The object should be evidence-bearing rather than merely metadata-rich. A claim is not useful because it has many fields, but because an inspector can follow why it was introduced, what supports it, what would oppose it, which transformations produced the current formulation, and what downstream conclusions depend on it. This creates a different design objective from the ordinary knowledge graph. The graph must preserve contestability and versioned reasons, not only relations that appear settled. Contradictions, alternative operationalizations, and unresolved status are first-class states rather than errors to be normalized away.
Epistemic version control should distinguish a textual edit from a scientific change. Rephrasing a paragraph may leave the claim invariant, while changing an inclusion criterion, causal assumption, measurement procedure, or evaluator can alter the meaning of every downstream result. A semantic commit should therefore identify the type of change, the evidence or decision that motivated it, and the branches that require reconsideration. The system may use language models to propose a diff, but acceptance requires domain-aware validation and the ability to display uncertainty when several interpretations remain plausible.
The living specification is the forward-looking counterpart of the semantic history. It records the question, rival hypotheses, admissible claims, controls, evidence obligations, budgets, stop conditions, safety constraints, and decision rights that currently govern the inquiry. It must remain revisable because research changes its own problem. The compiler is not expected to turn natural-language intent into a complete formal program. Its purpose is to expose missing commitments, produce candidate executable fragments, and preserve the relationship between the original intention and the actions later performed. an executable research representation, dynamic circuits, or a governed interpretation runtime may provide implementation experiments for this layer, but the hypothesis is independent of those technologies.

The same project would be represented conventionally and as an evidence-bearing object. The research question is not whether the richer interface feels impressive. It is whether it changes error discovery, reconstruction time, reviewer agreement, and the ability to explain why a claim changed.
The difficult issue is granularity. If every action becomes a provenance event, the object becomes unusable. If only final artefacts are preserved, the object reproduces the paper's compression. Research must identify which transitions are epistemically consequential and how this differs across domains. A semantic commit in a clinical study is not the same as one in theorem proving. The common layer may need a small vocabulary of claim transitions combined with domain-specific extensions.
Evaluation should include adversarial reconstruction. Independent teams can receive partial objects with selected provenance removed, contradictory branches inserted, or semantic changes obscured. The system succeeds only if inspectors can localize what is missing and if the representation improves their ability to detect consequential change compared with ordinary papers, notebooks, and repositories. 10.2 Corrective, Experimental, Formal, and Governance Infrastructure
The third family concerns criticism as infrastructure. Generation scales readily because one model can propose many candidates. Scientific resistance does not scale in the same way. Independent reproduction, causal challenge, specialist judgment, privacy review, copyright analysis, and ethical authorization require heterogeneous evidence and often different institutions. The central technical question is how to turn criticism from free-form commentary into typed, dependency-aware evidence without reducing judgment to a universal score.
Independent Critic Network
Create critics with distinct evidence sources, tools, model families, and authority; measure
whether dependency fingerprints predict correlated failure better than agent count or stated persona.
Severe-Test Design Agent Generate experiments targeted at named error modes and compare their information gain with conventional confirmatory proposals.

and purpose limitation; compare enforcement and usability across federated, synthetic, encrypted, and trusted-execution approaches.
A critic should be defined by the property it challenges and the evidence it can obtain, not by a theatrical persona. One critic may test statistical calibration, another reproduce an execution environment, another search for causal alternatives, and another inspect whether a claim exceeds the scope of its data. Their outputs should identify the target claim, the error mode, the procedure used, the result, the dependency fingerprint, and the consequence for the evidence state. Free-form prose can accompany the result, but it should not be the only artefact returned to the workbench.
The critic network should include deterministic checks, formal tools, independently implemented pipelines, specialist humans, and agents based on different models or corpora. Multiple prompts to the same foundation model do not create meaningful independence. Research should estimate correlated error by changing dependencies deliberately and observing which failures move together. A dependency fingerprint may include training lineage, retrieval source, code base, laboratory, operator, statistical library, instrument, funding interest, and institutional role. The goal is not an impossible proof of independence, but a decision-relevant account of shared vulnerability.
A severe-test agent begins from a named error that matters. It searches for an observation, intervention, counterexample, or replication design that would probably expose that error if it existed. This differs from asking for another experiment likely to produce a publishable effect. The agent must estimate what alternatives the test discriminates, what auxiliary assumptions it relies on, and what result would remain ambiguous. In formal domains, the severe test may be a counterexample search or independent proof. In empirical domains, it may be a holdout population, negative control, alternative instrument, or intervention that separates rival mechanisms.
Automated peer review should orchestrate these critics rather than imitate a conventional report. A claim-specific review graph can show which parts were checked, which remain unexamined, where critics disagree, and what evidence a rebuttal adds. Reviewers and authors should be able to challenge the critic's method and dependency, not merely its language. The system should preserve minority reports and the history of revisions so that later replication can revisit an unresolved objection. A single acceptance score would destroy much of the value created by this richer process.
Compliance is not an administrative appendix when it determines which data may be used, which experiments may be performed, and which results may be released. A configurable copilot can represent legal, ethical, copyright, contractual, and institutional rules together with their sources, jurisdiction, scope, conflicts, and required authority. Its output should distinguish clear prohibitions, conditional permissions, missing facts, and questions that require human interpretation. It should never convert regulatory ambiguity into a false scientific certainty.
The controlled-data agent applies these constraints to actual data flows. It can enforce purpose limitation, minimization, access conditions, retention, lineage, and privacy-preserving computation. Related approaches include federated learning, secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, trusted execution environments, synthetic data, and controlled analysis enclaves. The a privacy-governed data-use agent is one possible ScriptaHub implementation line. The research issue is not choosing a fashionable privacy technology, but determining whether the resulting evidence remains valid, auditable, and usable under the protection mechanism.
A promising integrated demonstrator is an automated validity dossier for an AI-assisted study. Generator agents produce candidate analyses, but independent critics use different retrieval services, execution environments, statistical tests, and model families. Their dependency fingerprints are visible. A peer-review orchestrator asks claim-specific questions, a compliance copilot checks the configured rules, and a controlled-data agent verifies purpose, minimization, and access. Human reviewers see disagreements and missing evidence rather than a single confidence score.

10.3 Institutional Design, Human Command, Integrated Demonstrators, and Revision
The fifth family concerns science as a social and political system. Pedigree, visibility, networks, capital, institutional authority, and platform ownership influence which questions receive attention and which failures remain visible. These forces cannot be eliminated by an algorithm, and expertise should not be flattened into anonymous voting. The research challenge is to design counterweights: blinded evaluation where appropriate, conflict and dependency graphs, protected exploratory portfolios, publication of informative failure, rights of appeal, plural funding mechanisms, and governance that keeps humans in command of consequence while allowing machines substantial local autonomy.
Project direction Core question and possible demonstrator
Pedigree and Power Quantify the influence of institution, network, geography, funding, and platform ownership
Anti-Monoculture Audit
Measure concentration of topics, datasets, citations, ontologies, evaluators, and model
families in AI-assisted science; test interventions that preserve plural search spaces.
Credit and Benefit Ledger Represent contributions by researchers, critics, agents, datasets, instruments, and communities, and study rules for attribution, licensing, revenue, and public benefit that remain open to appeal.
Human-Command Constitution Define decision rights by capability, consequence, domain, and evidence; test whether users can genuinely stop, revise, and understand consequential automated processes rather than merely approve them ceremonially.
A pedigree-and-power audit should show how attention, funding, review, infrastructure, and model access are distributed. It can combine citation and collaboration networks with grant histories, institutional affiliation, geography, ownership, data access, model dependencies, and reviewer relations. The purpose is not to calculate a moral ranking of institutions or individuals. It is to identify concentrations and feedback loops that may make some claims sociologically difficult to falsify or some alternatives unable to receive a serious test.
Counterfactual analysis can estimate how decisions change when status signals are altered, while qualitative research examines why participants rely on those signals. The audit should preserve legitimate explanations such as rare expertise or facility access and distinguish them from inherited visibility. It should also expose the pedigree of AI systems: their training corpora, platform ownership, benchmark communities, and model lineages. An automated evaluator can reproduce hierarchy even when names are hidden because prestige remains encoded in citation structure and textual style.
These projects require mixed methods. Large-scale bibliometric and network analysis can identify concentration, but it cannot determine fairness or scientific significance by itself. Controlled review experiments can test blinding, structured criteria, and alternative funding mechanisms. Ethnographic and interview work can reveal how scientists actually use AI systems, where authority shifts, and which forms of oversight become ceremonial. Institutional prototypes can test appeal, minority reports, negative-result credit, and benefit-sharing in real collaborations.
Institutional simulation can examine how small changes in incentives alter long-term scientific diversity. Models can compare publication rewards, replication budgets, threshold lotteries, portfolio diversity constraints, open failure archives, and different intellectual-property regimes. Such simulations do not predict institutions mechanically. They generate hypotheses and reveal hidden assumptions for field experiments. The relevant outcomes include concentration, correction time, survival of minority programmes, duplicated effort, reproducibility, and the distribution of risk and benefit.
An anti-monoculture monitor should analyze common dependencies across a portfolio. A hundred projects may use different titles while relying on the same foundation model, benchmark, ontology, data provider, and evaluation rule. Conversely, two superficially similar projects may explore genuinely different mechanisms. The monitor should represent this difference and help allocate resources to independent evaluators, alternative datasets, underexplored populations, and competing representations. It should not become a novelty score that researchers learn to game.
The human-command constitution should be expressed as operational rights. People must know which decisions are theirs, receive evidence in a form suitable to those decisions, possess adequate time and competence, be able to stop or revise the process, and have access to an appeal path. A click-to-approve interface does not meet this condition. Nor does a committee that is formally responsible but lacks access to the relevant provenance or the power to change the system. The research question is whether authority can be made both effective and compatible with substantial local machine autonomy.
Appeal must be designed as part of the architecture rather than added after a controversial decision. Affected researchers and communities need access to the relevant evidence, dependency graph, policy basis, and decision history. The appeal body must possess authority to change the result and protection from the same conflicts that shaped the original decision. Research should measure correction, delay, accessibility, strategic abuse, and whether weaker actors can use the process in practice rather than only in principle.
Benefit attribution can be prototyped alongside contribution tracking. spans.quote:
Introduction. The Scientific Machine That Must Learn to Correct Itself
The conventional promise of artificial intelligence for science is acceleration. Models will read more papers, generate more hypotheses, write more code, run more simulations, and help laboratories work continuously. These capabilities matter, but speed is the least distinctive and potentially the most misleading part of the transition. A process can accelerate while moving through the wrong conceptual space, optimizing a contaminated benchmark, repeating a hidden causal mistake, or producing claims faster than any institution can test them.
The more consequential change is a reversal of scarcity. Scientific institutions developed in a world where producing a candidate result consumed enough labour to limit the number of branches a team could pursue. AI weakens that filter. As hypotheses, analyses, implementations, and manuscripts become cheaper, the scarce functions migrate toward judgment: deciding which questions deserve physical resources, which evidence discriminates among live explanations, whether criticism is independent, what must be remembered after a failed branch, and who may release or act on a claim.
This is why the programme is organized around correction rather than generation. Its technology concepts are not justified by novelty alone. Each is tied to a failure that becomes more dangerous under automation: the paper loses the branching history of inquiry; embeddings collapse different kinds of idea identity; correlated agents simulate consensus; benchmark gains substitute for explanatory progress; privacy and compliance are added after architecture rather than shaping it; prestige and ownership determine attention before evidence is inspected; and humans remain nominally in the loop while real authority moves into opaque infrastructure.
The programme does not assume that every scientific activity should be automated or that every domain can be evaluated by the same oracle. It asks where automation can make a bounded contribution: retrieving evidence, preserving alternatives, generating counterexamples, executing protocols, designing discriminating experiments, checking claims, tracing dependencies, enforcing policy, or exposing the power relations that distort selection. The aim is to automate as much scientifically useful work as possible while leaving people genuinely at the helm: able to set purposes, constrain means, contest judgments, stop consequential actions, and benefit from the results.
spans.sectionHeading: Introduction. The Scientific Machine That Must Learn to Correct Itself

spans.quote:
The Claim That Arrived Before Its Evidence
A discovery can now be generated, executed, narrated, and reviewed before science has
established what is new, what caused the result, who independently checked it, or who has
authority to act.
At 08:10, a research system identifies what appears to be an unexplored relation in a scientific corpus. By 09:40 it has translated the relation into a mechanism. Before noon it has written code, selected data, and produced a promising result. In a digitally native field, or in a tightly automated laboratory, it may also execute a sequence of experiments. By evening it has generated figures, a manuscript, a novelty statement, and several reviews produced by other agents. The next morning the result is described as a discovery.
Nothing in this thought experiment requires a mythical general intelligence. Every operation already exists in partial form: scientific retrieval, hypothesis generation, code execution, theorem search, active experimental design, robotic control, manuscript production, and automated criticism. The unusual feature is their speed and composition. The result can acquire the complete surface of science before any person or institution has reconstructed the path beneath it.
What, exactly, arrived at 08:10? Was the relation new to the model, new to the indexed corpus, new to one discipline, or new to science? Did the code test the intended mechanism or a convenient proxy? Was the experiment decisive, or did the system choose a region in which its evaluator was easiest to satisfy? Were the reviews independent, or did every agent inherit the same corpus, model family, and blind spot? Which failed branches disappeared from the manuscript? Who is prepared to sign the claim, authorize its use, and accept the consequences if it is wrong?
The system has not necessarily produced a discovery. It has produced a candidate scientific package whose appearance is more complete than its epistemic status. This mismatch is the central condition of the coming era. Artificial intelligence lowers the cost of candidate science more quickly than it lowers the cost of deciding which candidates deserve belief.
Modern scientific institutions were built under a different scarcity. A hypothesis, implementation, experiment, and paper consumed enough human labour that production itself constrained volume. This filter excluded unconventional ideas and preserved many inequalities, but it also limited the number of branches that demanded attention. A generative system can remove the cost of proposing a branch without removing the cost of understanding it, designing a decisive test, reproducing it independently, or taking responsibility for release.
Science is therefore entering a validation economy. The scarce resources are no longer only ideas, code, or prose. They are criticism that can change the fate of a claim, experiments that separate live explanations, specialists who can judge a narrow unresolved question, laboratories whose errors are materially independent, and institutions willing to own a consequential decision. The scientific value of automation should be measured by the quality-adjusted rate at which claims acquire independent support or are efficiently rejected, not by the number of candidate papers a system can produce.
This reverses the usual image of progress. The most valuable system may be the one that generates fewer final claims because it discovers earlier that an effect comes from leakage, calibration drift, extra compute, a weak baseline, or an invalid operational definition. A negative control that closes a branch can be more valuable than an additional positive experiment. A critic that exposes a shared dependency can contribute more than a chorus of agreeing agents. The rate of correction becomes more informative than the rate of narration.
The danger is not only hallucination. It is the mechanical research loop: a process that remains locally competent while optimizing a proxy that has drifted from the purpose of inquiry. The literature agent finds plausible sources. The planner proposes a sensible experiment. The coding agent produces a working repository. The evaluator reports improvement. The reviewer praises clarity. Every local step can appear successful while the system has silently changed the question or selected an evaluator that cannot distinguish the proposed mechanism from a simpler explanation.
The first requirement of future science is therefore not greater confidence but organized resistance. A scientific system must be able to state what would change its conclusion, expose where an evaluator is weak, preserve rival explanations, and stop when continued optimization no longer serves the original purpose. This is the meaning of the title: the frontier is correction because reliable intelligence is not the absence of error. It is the architecture through which error becomes visible, consequential, and reversible.
Return to the morning claim. Its first unresolved property is novelty. A language model can report that it did not retrieve an equivalent phrase. An embedding system can report that the proposal lies far from familiar documents. Neither result establishes that the underlying idea lacks a precedent. The same mechanism can migrate across fields under different terminology. A recent method can repeat an old principle while adding the first effective implementation. A contribution can be mostly inherited and still become important by removing one restrictive assumption.
Newness is not a substance attached to the candidate. It is a relation among the candidate, a memory, a representation, an equivalence rule, a time, and a community. Change the corpus and the priority claim can change. Change the level of abstraction and a method can become old in mechanism but new in evidence. Change the comparison question and two contributions can become the same for one purpose and different for another.
Identity must therefore be typed

spans.quote:
Chapter 3. Evidence-Carrying Research Objects and the Executable Record
Automation exposes a representational failure at the centre of contemporary science. The paper is an extraordinarily successful public argument, but it is a poor durable record of a branching, computational, agentic inquiry. The technology concepts in this chapter begin from a different
unit: an evidence-carrying research object with versioned claims, assumptions, artefacts,
decisions, negative results, and permissions. Such an object requires a theory of novelty and
identity that is typed rather than reduced to document similarity, and it requires living
specifications that can expand into rival hypotheses, controls, replications, and tests while
retaining the reasons for every change.
spans.sectionHeading: Chapter 3. Evidence-Carrying Research Objects and the Executable Record

spans.quote:
Chapter 10. From Principles to Technology Concepts: The Research Portfolio
The final chapter converts the preceding arguments into a portfolio of researchable technology families. The objective is not to freeze a product architecture. It is to state the missing layer, the scientific reason for believing that the layer matters, the artefact that could embody the idea, the relations to neighbouring components, the evaluator regime, and the observations that would
force revision. The programme should be judged by whether these formulations make future
projects more precise and falsifiable, not by whether every proposed name survives
implementation.
